nssdca-moon.label: NASA NSSDCA, Table of Anthropogenic Impacts and Spacecraft on the Moon (public domain)
nssdca-moon.says: NASA NSSDCA, 'Table of Anthropogenic Impacts and Spacecraft on the Moon' (D. R. Williams, last updated 13 August 2025): 96 rows, each with a landing or impact date and a latitude and longitude (N and E positive) where one is known. Public domain (NASA). The generator reads the table itself; this key is cited by its rows.

wikipedia-geodata.label: Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0): the coordinates each mission's article carries
wikipedia-geodata.says: The coordinates Wikipedia's articles carry on a named globe (MediaWiki GeoData, CC BY-SA 4.0), read through the API for the article of each mission. Whole degrees where the article gives whole degrees. They are the articles' figures, which cite NSSDCA and the papers of Bindschadler, Head and Garvin (1986) and Abdrakhimov and Basilevsky (2002); the mission pages of NSSDCA were not used because the Venus sites they name carry no coordinates.

wikipedia-missions.label: Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0): the article on the mission
wikipedia-missions.says: The lead of each article named, read through Wikipedia's REST summary on 29 October 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0): the missions' dates and what each did. No coordinate for a small body was found in a source we could read, so none is given except DART's.

daly-2023.label: Daly et al. 2023, Nature 616, 443, Table 1
daly-2023.says: Daly et al. 2023, Nature 616, 443, Table 1: the DART impact site on Dimorphos, 8.84 +/- 0.45 degrees S, 264.30 +/- 0.47 degrees E (east longitude, the IAU prime meridian of the asteroid; planetocentric or planetographic latitude is not stated).

esa-schiaparelli.label: Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0): Schiaparelli EDM
esa-schiaparelli.says: Wikipedia's Schiaparelli EDM carries 2.05 S, 353.79 E, the crash site found in Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's CTX picture of 20 October 2016.

wikipedia-tianwen-2.label: Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0): Tianwen-2
wikipedia-tianwen-2.says: Wikipedia, Tianwen-2 (CC BY-SA 4.0), read 29 October 2026: launched 28 May 2025; 'rendezvoused with Kamoʻoalewa in July 2026' (4 July), approached within 20 km; 'conducting remote sensing observations in orbit, while scouting for a sampling site'; planned to leave 24 April 2027 and release its return capsule on 29 November 2027.

esa-mmx.label: ESA: MMX lifts off to Mars's moon Phobos
esa-mmx.says: ESA, 'MMX lifts off to Mars's moon Phobos': launched on a JAXA H3 rocket from Tanegashima at 04:41 JST on 20 October 2026; arrives at Mars 'next summer'; the first spacecraft to orbit Phobos, the first to collect samples from its surface and the first to return to Earth from the Mars system.

rows.name: Venera 4, end of descent
rows.doing: Sent the first measurements from inside the air of another planet, and went silent before it reached the ground.

rows.name: Venera 5, end of descent
rows.doing: Fell through the air of Venus in May 1969 and went silent before it reached the ground.

rows.name: Venera 6, end of descent
rows.doing: The twin of Venera 5, a day later: it too went silent before it reached the surface.

rows.name: Venera 7 landing site
rows.doing: The first soft landing on another planet, and the first data sent from the ground of one.

rows.name: Venera 8 landing site
rows.doing: The second probe to land on Venus, and the first to land on its sunlit side.

rows.name: Venera 9 landing site
rows.doing: Sent the first picture from the ground of another planet, a slope strewn with rocks.

rows.name: Venera 10 landing site
rows.doing: Landed three days after its twin, Venera 9, and sent a picture of its own.

rows.name: Venera 11 landing site
rows.doing: Landed and measured the air and the soil, but its camera caps did not come off, so there is no picture.

rows.name: Venera 12 landing site
rows.doing: Landed four days before Venera 11 and worked on the ground; its camera caps stayed on too.

rows.name: Venera 13 landing site
rows.doing: Sent the first colour pictures from the ground of another planet and analysed a sample it drilled.

rows.name: Venera 14 landing site
rows.doing: Landed four days after Venera 13 and sent pictures and a soil analysis of its own.

rows.name: VEGA 1 lander
rows.doing: Dropped its lander and a balloon into the air of Venus on the way to Halley's comet.

rows.name: VEGA 2 lander
rows.doing: Landed four days after VEGA 1 and analysed the soil. Two figures for the place, two degrees apart, are in print.

rows.name: Pioneer Venus Large Probe, entry
rows.doing: The big probe of Pioneer Venus, 315 kg, sent data all the way down through the air; it was not built to land.

rows.name: Pioneer Venus North Probe, entry
rows.doing: A small probe sent into the high northern air of Venus, one of four dropped on one day.

rows.name: Pioneer Venus Day Probe, landing
rows.doing: Not built to land, it kept sending for more than an hour after it hit the ground.

rows.name: Pioneer Venus Night Probe, entry
rows.doing: A small probe sent into the night side of Venus. Like the others except the Day Probe, it was not built to survive the ground.

rows.name: Mars 2 crash site
rows.doing: The first thing from Earth to reach the ground of Mars, and it hit it hard: its landing system failed. Where, is known to a few degrees.

rows.name: Mars 6, lost at landing
rows.doing: Sent data on the way down and went silent as it reached the ground. Where it came down is from tracking, to a few degrees.

rows.name: Beagle 2
rows.doing: Landed on Christmas Day 2003 and was never heard from. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter found it in 2015, with its panels not all open.

rows.name: Schiaparelli crash site
rows.doing: ESA's test lander fell from about 3.7 km when its thrusters stopped early. The scar is in Meridiani Planum, photographed from orbit the next day.

rows.name: NEAR Shoemaker, Eros
rows.doing: The first landing on an asteroid. NEAR Shoemaker was not built to land, and it sent data for two weeks from the ground.

rows.name: Hayabusa, Itokawa
rows.doing: Touched down twice on a small rubble-pile asteroid in November 2005, and brought back its dust in 2010.

rows.name: Hayabusa2, Ryugu
rows.doing: Touched down on Ryugu in February and July 2019, the second time beside a crater it had made, and brought the samples home in 2020.

rows.name: OSIRIS-REx, Bennu
rows.doing: Touched Bennu for six seconds at a site called Nightingale and took in so much dust that the sample box would not close.

rows.name: Philae, comet 67P
rows.doing: The first landing on a comet. Philae bounced twice off Churyumov-Gerasimenko and came to rest in a shadow, where its batteries ran out.

rows.name: Rosetta, end of mission
rows.doing: Ended its twelve years by coming down slowly on comet 67P, sending pictures until just before it touched.

rows.name: DART impact site, Dimorphos
rows.doing: NASA's DART spacecraft hit this asteroid moon at 6 km a second and shortened its orbit round Didymos by more than half an hour.

rows.name: Deep Impact impactor, comet Tempel 1
rows.doing: A 370 kg copper impactor hit the comet at 10 km a second while the mother ship watched.

rows.name: Tianwen-2, Kamoʻoalewa
rows.doing: China's Tianwen-2 reached this small asteroid in July 2026 and is looking for a place to take a sample. It is due to leave in April 2027 and send a capsule home that November.

rows.name: MMX, Phobos
rows.doing: Japan's MMX left Earth on 20 October 2026 for Mars. It will be the first craft to orbit Phobos, to take a sample from it, and to come back from the Mars system.
